EU-27 Green-Transition Typology: Design & Results

Vulnerability × Potential map — self-contained reproduction for review

1 Research question & motivation

  • Project (WP1, OPUS “Green transition & economic polarization in Europe”). Build a national taxonomy of the EU-27 that captures how well-placed each Member State is for the green transition, and ask whether the transition risks reinforcing existing core–periphery polarization.
  • Design (proposal Fig. 1). Two vulnerabilities (transition burden) and two potentials (green capability), placed on a 2-D vulnerability × potential map with four quadrants (Winners / Exposed / Low-stakes / At risk).
  • Guiding requirements for the axes:
    • Each axis must be distinct from the other and not merely a proxy for GDP per capita — but income relevance is expected and welcome, not something to engineer away.
    • The axes must differentiate countries (a visible growth-model story), else there is nothing to build a narrative on.
    • No double-counting: two near-identical indicators should not silently dominate a block.

2 Method

2.1 Indicators (six, two per dimension)

  • Vulnerability
    • Emission intensity of production — carbon intensity (GHG / value added) and energy intensity (final energy / value added).
    • Fossil dependency — fossil share of gross available energy (demand side).
  • Potential
    • Green economic complexity — GCI (current green export complexity) and GCP (connectedness / potential to diversify into green products).
    • Green innovation — green patents per capita.

2.2 Fossil share: demand-side, not production-side

  • The fossil share is measured on gross available energy (what a country consumes), replacing the earlier fossil share of primary production (what it extracts). The two barely agree (r = 0.34).
Production- vs demand-based fossil share (selected).
country fossil (production) fossil (gross avail.)
Germany 0.43 0.82
Denmark 0.73 0.69
Estonia 0.00 0.86
Ireland 0.37 0.91
Luxembourg 0.00 0.83
Malta 0.00 0.96
  • The production measure is 0 for every non-producer (Malta, Luxembourg, Baltics) and even mis-codes oil-shale Estonia — an artifact. The demand measure captures actual fossil dependence and has full EU-27 coverage.

2.3 Scoring: two-part axes (twin sub-index + standalone)

  • Within each block the two intensity / two complexity indicators are strongly correlated — they are two facets of one construct, not independent variables.
Within-block correlations: the twins cohere; the standalone is distinct.
pair correlation
carbon intensity ↔︎ energy intensity 0.68
GCI ↔︎ GCP 0.78
intensity twins ↔︎ fossil 0.07
complexity twins ↔︎ patents 0.18
  • So each axis is built in two steps: (1) reduce the correlated twin pair to a single sub-index (first principal component); (2) combine that sub-index with the standalone indicator at equal weight (standardised mean). This treats the two parts as co-equal conceptual dimensions, so neither the twin pair (2 indicators) nor the standalone (1 indicator) dominates by count.
  • Contrast with a flat PCA over all three variables per block: there the correlated twins dominate PC1 and the standalone loads only ~0.14–0.28, i.e. is almost ignored.

3 Results

3.1 Axes are distinct, differentiating, and income-balanced

Go/no-go and differentiation diagnostics (structured axes).
metric value
cor(vulnerability, potential) -0.57
R² vulnerability ~ log GDP p.c. 0.25
R² potential ~ log GDP p.c. 0.33
eta² vulnerability ~ growth model 0.37
eta² potential ~ growth model 0.44
  • Distinct axes: cor(vulnerability, potential) = −0.57 — related (high burden tends to pair with low capability) but far from ±1, so not one axis in disguise.
  • Income present but balanced: both R²(~log GDP) are moderate (0.25 / 0.33). Income matters in both blocks, dominates neither. This is by design: within each block one part is income-linked and one income-neutral, on opposite diagonals (intensity & patents track GDP; fossil & complexity do not).
  • Differentiation: eta² (variance explained by growth model) is high on both axes — the core–periphery structure is clearly visible.

4 Validation

4.1 External validity: do the axes predict what they should?

The scores are validated against outcomes not used to build them, controlling for income (partial correlation net of log GDP p.c.): the overall renewable share (Eurostat SHARES REN), real GDP growth over the window, and the OECD Environmental Policy Stringency index (EPS, 20/27 countries).

Correlation of each axis with external validators (partial = net of log GDP p.c.).
score outcome raw_cor partial_cor
vulnerability renew_share -0.46 -0.51
vulnerability gdp_growth 0.27 0.17
vulnerability eps -0.39 -0.39
potential renew_share 0.25 0.36
potential gdp_growth -0.55 -0.42
potential eps 0.58 0.63
  • Expected signs hold: potential is positively associated with the renewable share, growth and policy stringency; vulnerability negatively — and the associations survive controlling for income.
  • Circularity flag: fossil dependency is ~half of vulnerability and the fossil share is ~ (1 − renewable share), so vulnerability ~ renewable share is partly mechanical — read it as descriptive. Renewable share remains a clean validator for potential (which contains no fossil term).

4.2 Relation to the development-model classification

The central polarization question is how the green-transition typology relates to the Gräbner et al. (2020) European growth-model classification: Core (DE, AT, BE, DK, FI, SE), Finance (LU, NL, MT, IE), Periphery (FR, GR, IT, PT, ES, CY), Workbench (the eastern catch-up economies).

Mean axis scores by growth-model group.
Growth model n vulnerability potential
Core 6 -1.02 1.19
Periphery 6 -0.06 -0.14
Finance 4 0.10 -0.31
Workbench 11 0.55 -0.46
Quadrant × growth model (Cramér’s V = 0.45; descriptive, n = 27).
Core Finance Periphery Workbench
At risk 0 2 2 7
Exposed 0 1 0 2
Low-stakes 0 0 1 1
Winners 6 1 3 1
  • The typology tracks the development model, but does not reproduce it (Cramér’s V moderate, not 1): growth model and transition quadrant are clearly associated, yet the mapping is many-to-many.
  • Core → mostly Winners; Workbench → mostly At risk — the transition risks reinforcing the existing core–periphery divide (the polarization hypothesis).
  • But the typology adds resolution the development model lacks:
    • Finance splits — clean, high-innovation Luxembourg → Winners vs. fossil-dependent, low-complexity Malta / Ireland → At risk.
    • Periphery splits — larger economies (IT, ES) sit near Winners while Portugal drops toward Low-stakes.
    • Within Workbench, coal-heavy Poland / Czechia are Exposed (real burden) while cleaner Slovakia is Low-stakes — a distinction the single development-model label hides.

5 Robustness

5.1 Stability to the aggregation choice

The headline combines each block as a twin sub-index + standalone. As an alternative, each block can be reduced by a single PCA over all three variables (which lets the correlated twins dominate). The map is stable to this choice:

Countries differing between single-PCA blocks and the structured axes (8 of 27).
country group single PCA structured
Finland Core Exposed Winners
Ireland Finance Low-stakes At risk
Luxembourg Finance Low-stakes Winners
Malta Finance Low-stakes At risk
Netherlands Finance Winners Exposed
Portugal Periphery Winners Low-stakes
Slovakia Workbench At risk Low-stakes
Slovenia Workbench Exposed Winners
  • Only 8 of 27 countries differ, so the classification is not an artifact of the aggregation rule.
  • The differences are interpretable: the structured axes give the standalone dimensions real weight, so high-innovation economies (Luxembourg, Slovenia, Finland) and fossil-dependent ones (Malta, Ireland) are placed on their own merits rather than being absorbed by the correlated twins.
  • Further checks in 07_robustness.R, all against the structured headline, are reassuring: the twin sub-index as a mean instead of PC1 (0/27), robust scaling (2/27), ECI for GCI (0/27), renewable-only GCI (2/27), indicator-window shifts (0/27) and single-country drops (1/26). The map moves most under the two genuine measurement choices — flat aggregation (8/27) and the production-based fossil share (8/27) — which is why both are argued for explicitly in the Method.

6 Interpretation

  • The transition risks reinforcing polarization — this is the headline finding. Core economies cluster in Winners, the Workbench East in At risk: those least equipped for the transition (low green capability) also carry a real transition burden. Green-transition standing and development-model position are strongly associated.
  • …but the typology is a refinement of the development model, not a relabelling. The association is moderate (Cramér’s V < 1), and the map resolves within-group heterogeneity the single development-model label hides: Finance splits (Luxembourg vs Malta/Ireland), Periphery splits (IT/ES vs Portugal), and the Workbench separates coal-burdened (PL, CZ) from lower-stakes (SK) economies.
  • The taxonomy is not “just income.” Both axes carry a moderate, balanced income signal (R² 0.25 / 0.33) — present by design, dominating neither — and they are clearly distinct (cor −0.57), so the map is not a GDP ranking in disguise.
  • Each block measures two genuine dimensions. A coherent two-indicator construct (emission intensity; green complexity) is combined at equal weight with a distinct standalone (fossil dependency; green innovation). This gives fossil dependency and innovation full standing, which is what places Malta/Ireland (fossil-locked, low complexity) in At risk and the innovation leaders in Winners.
  • Caveats to keep in view.
    • Fossil dependency is ~half of vulnerability and the fossil share is ~ (1 − renewable share), so the renewable-share validator is partly circular for vulnerability (r = −0.46) — read it as descriptive there; it stays a clean validator for potential, alongside GDP growth and policy stringency.
    • Quadrants come from median splits; countries near an axis median are convention-sensitive (flagged as borderline in 04_typology.R). ```
